title: Days and Time Words
description: Today, tomorrow, yesterday and now; the parts of the day people actually use; the day that matters (Friday); and متى — the question that puts everything on a clock.
approach: A day strip and a week strip on screen: each time word highlights its slot as it is heard; the learner then narrates a simple day (morning, noon, night) and answers متى؟ with the words.
unlock_condition: ≥11/15 on the timeline tap quiz and a recorded answer to متى؟
can_do: Say today, tomorrow, yesterday and now
Name the parts of the day and the days that matter

grammar.title: متى؟ — when
grammar.explanation: متى asks when, and it works with a thing as well as a verb: متى الغدا؟ when is lunch, متى الدوام؟ when is work. The answer is one of this lesson's words, often with إن شاء الله attached if it is in the future: باكر إن شاء الله. For clock time you ask الساعة كم؟ — how much is the hour — and answer with a number from Lesson 6: الساعة خمسة.

examples.arabic: متى نشوفك؟ — باكر إن شاء الله
examples.transliteration: mita nshuufak? — baakir in shaaʾ allaah
examples.english: When will we see you? — Tomorrow, God willing
What time is it? — Seven o'clock
When is work? — In the morning

grammar.title: Time words go first or last — not in the middle
grammar.explanation: A time word sits at the front of the sentence or at the very end, and the sentence is the same either way: اليوم أنا بالبيت or أنا بالبيت اليوم. Putting it first makes the time the topic (as for today…); putting it last just adds it. Fixed times take the article — الصبح, الليل, الجمعة — and the prayer-anchored ones are used like clock times: بعد المغرب is a perfectly normal appointment.

examples.english: On Friday lunch is at my grandmother's

culture.title: The day is shaped by five prayers
culture.note: People tell time by the prayers as much as by the clock: الفجر (dawn), الظهر (noon), العصر (afternoon), المغرب (sunset), العشا (night). 'After maghrib' is an ordinary time to meet, and evening visits begin then. In Saudi shops used to close briefly at every prayer; most now stay open, but a cashier may still step away. Lunch is late (2–4pm) and the evening starts late (9pm is early for a visit), so a Gulf 'morning' is the only early part of the day.

culture.title: Friday is the week
culture.note: The week turns on الجمعة: Friday prayer at noon, then the big family lunch, usually at the grandparents'. The weekend is Friday and Saturday everywhere in the Gulf now (it used to be Thursday–Friday, and older people still say it). The working week starts Sunday, so 'Monday morning' feelings arrive on الأحد. Shops open late in the morning and stay open late at night; the busiest hours of a mall are after 9pm.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'the day' — the article makes it 'today'. Gulf also says هاليوم (this day). Never the Egyptian النهاردة. Stress on the last syllable: il-YAWM.
vocabulary.image_scene: A wall calendar with today's date circled in red, sunlight on it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Vlog openings: اليوم بنروح…; the day's plan announced.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the Emirates say باكر — and pronounce it baachir with the ch. Saudis say بكرة bukra. Both are accepted; you will hear both in the first week of video. Nearly always followed by إن شاء الله.
vocabulary.image_scene: A calendar page being turned to the next day, a sunrise icon on it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Plans for the next day at the end of a vlog; باكر / بكرة with إن شاء الله.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Short and universal in the Gulf. البارحة (last night / yesterday) is the other common word; Jeddah says أمبارح. Never امبارح in the Egyptian sense of a habit — just recognise it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A calendar with the previous day crossed off, a faded photo beside it.

example.english: Yesterday I was at the souq

vocabulary.video_hint: Recaps at the start of a vlog: أمس رحنا…

vocabulary.teaching_note: Understood from Kuwait to Fujairah: il-ḥiin. Very often هالحين (this now); Jeddah says دحين. The MSA الآن is never said in speech and the Egyptian دلوقتي never in the Gulf.
vocabulary.image_scene: A clock face with the hands at the moment, a finger tapping the glass.
vocabulary.video_hint: الحين / هالحين in any live narration; شتسوي الحين on the phone.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Later on, or 'then' in a sequence. Kuwait, Bahrain and the Emirates also say عقب; 'in a bit' is بعد شوي. The polite way to put something off: بعدين إن شاء الله.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand gesturing 'later' with a small wave, a clock in the background showing a later hour.
vocabulary.video_hint: Deferring something in a sketch; sequences narrated with بعدين.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The morning as a time: الصبح, in the morning. The greeting word صباح is the same root. Emphatic ص makes the u dark. من الصبح — since this morning.
vocabulary.image_scene: Early sun over a Gulf skyline, a man with a coffee cup on a balcony.
vocabulary.video_hint: Morning-routine vlogs; the first line of a day-in-the-life.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Night, and 'at night' is بالليل. One night is ليلة. The Gulf evening starts late, so بالليل can mean anything up to two in the morning.
vocabulary.image_scene: A quiet street at night with a crescent moon and lit windows.
vocabulary.video_hint: Night outings; a camp fire; الليلة for tonight.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A day. كل يوم every day, يومين two days, أيام days. The names of the days are built on it (يوم الجمعة). In Gulf storytelling يوم also means 'when' — a later lesson.
vocabulary.image_scene: A sun arcing over a house from sunrise to sunset in one image.

example.english: Every day, coffee in the morning

vocabulary.video_hint: كل يوم in routine vlogs; counting days of a trip.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said usbuuʿ, ending in ع. هالأسبوع this week; next week is الأسبوع الجاي. Plural أسابيع.
vocabulary.image_scene: A week-view calendar page with seven boxes, Friday highlighted.
vocabulary.video_hint: Weekly plans; الأسبوع الجاي at the end of a vlog.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Gulf says daayim (or دايماً) where MSA has دائماً with a hamza. Also 'permanent': سفرة دايمة — may your table always be laid — the blessing after a meal. على طول can also mean always.
vocabulary.image_scene: A repeating loop icon over a daily coffee cup, the same scene four times.

example.english: I always drink coffee in the morning

vocabulary.video_hint: Habits described in routine vlogs; دايم as an intensifier.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Used as-is in Gulf speech, often as أحيان. The more colloquial مرات (some times) does the same job — مرات أروح, sometimes I go. Written with or without the final alif.
vocabulary.image_scene: A calendar with a few random days ticked and the rest blank.
vocabulary.video_hint: Habits with exceptions; مرات in casual speech.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The when-question, said mita with a short i. Works with a thing or a verb: متى الغدا؟ متى تروح؟. Some Saudis say امتى. Not to be confused with يوم / لما, which mean 'when' in a story, not a question.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man tapping his wrist where a watch would be, eyebrows raised in question.
vocabulary.video_hint: Scheduling in dialogues; متى نروح؟ before an outing.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The day of the week that matters: prayer at noon, then the family lunch. Kuwaitis say il-yimʿa (ج → y). The other days: السبت, الأحد, الاثنين, الثلاثاء, الأربعا, الخميس — recognise them now, learn them in Stage 2.
vocabulary.image_scene: A large family lunch on a floor sufra, a mosque visible through the window, midday light.

example.english: On Friday lunch is at my family's

vocabulary.video_hint: Friday lunch vlogs; جمعة مباركة greetings.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Noon, named for the prayer. Said iẕ-ẕuhur with a helping vowel and the heavy ظ. Lunch is 'at ẕuhur' even when it is at three. بعد الظهر — afternoon.
vocabulary.image_scene: The sun directly overhead over a mosque courtyard, short shadows.
vocabulary.video_hint: The noon call to prayer; lunch announced.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sunset, and the everyday appointment time: بعد المغرب, after maghrib, is when visits and outings start. Contains غ, the gargled g — different from the خ of خبز.
vocabulary.image_scene: An orange sunset behind a minaret, lights coming on in the street.
vocabulary.video_hint: Sunset call to prayer; plans made for after maghrib.

dialogue.speaker: Fahad

dialogue.speaker: Fahad

dialogue.transliteration: ee, baʿd il-maghrib. wil-jumʿa l-ghada ʿind jaddati

sound_spotlight.explanation: The heavy th — the voiced ذ made with the tongue raised at the back. Gulf uses this sound for both ظ and ض, so once you have it you have two letters. Compare هذا (light) with الظهر (heavy).
Two back-of-the-throat sounds: غ is voiced, like gargling; خ is the same place but breathy, like clearing the throat. Sunset has the first; Thursday has the second.
Up the Gulf the k in باكر turns into ch — baachir — and some write it باچر. Saudis avoid the word and say بكرة. Recognise all three as tomorrow.

lesson_sequence.detail: A day strip (dawn to night) and a week strip with Friday marked. One line of English: today you put things on the clock. Tap يلّا.
Fifteen cards; each time word highlights its slot on the day or week strip as it plays. Tap any slot to hear its word again.
Three-day carousel; audio plays and the learner swipes to the right day. Then the learner records each word with the day on screen.
A native asks متى + something (الغدا, الدوام, نشوفك); the learner records an answer from the strip. The speech check listens for the time word.
A sentence card with a gap at the front and at the end; the learner drops the time word in either slot and hears both versions.
The scheduling dialogue plays with the strips animating; second pass the learner takes Khalid's lines.
Fifteen items: slot tap, متى answers, day-of-week recognition. Counter rolls to 135. Nudge: say the time word for whatever you are doing, three times today.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Right now, say الحين + where you are: الحين أنا بالبيت. Then say what is باكر.
real_world_prompts.context: Lesson-complete screen. Here-and-now time framing with known places.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tonight, look at the sunset and say المغرب. Tomorrow morning, say الصبح with your first coffee.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day notification. Ties two prayer-time words to real moments.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask your tutor five متى questions about their week and repeat each answer back.
real_world_prompts.context: Before a tutor session. The question plus its answer set, in real time.

video_needs.scene: A vlogger narrating their day with time words — الصبح, الظهر, بعد المغرب, بالليل — and morning-routine videos; اليوم / أمس / باكر in openings and sign-offs.
